title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 2
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: Hollis General Hospital installed alcohol-gel dispensers outside every ward in January. Reported hospital-acquired infections for the following year fell by 22 per cent compared with the previous year. Hospital management concluded that the dispensers had reduced infection.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Some staff reported that the dispensers were occasionally empty.
B. Other hospitals that installed dispensers reported similar reductions.
C. In the same January, the hospital changed from recording every suspected infection to recording only laboratory-confirmed ones.
D. The dispensers cost less than the treatment of a single serious infection.
E. Handwashing with soap remains more effective than gel against certain organisms.
questions.explanation: If the counting rule changed at the same moment, the fall may be in what was recorded rather than in what occurred — the two years are no longer comparable. A weakens the mechanism only slightly; C strengthens; D and E are irrelevant to whether infections actually fell.

questions.prompt: The city of Ardwick will introduce a charge for driving into its centre, arguing that the charge will reduce the concentration of nitrogen dioxide measured at its central monitoring stations.
questions.question: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Drivers deterred by the charge will not simply shift their journeys to routes that still affect the central monitoring stations.
B. The revenue raised will be spent on public transport.
C. Nitrogen dioxide is the most harmful pollutant present in the city centre.
D. Other cities that have introduced such charges have seen air quality improve.
E. The charge will be set high enough to cover the cost of collecting it.
questions.explanation: If deterred traffic reroutes around the centre in a way that still raises readings at those stations, the measured concentration need not fall. A, D and E concern desirability or precedent, not the logical requirement; B concerns which pollutant matters, not whether this one declines.

questions.prompt: A bakery has switched to a flour milled from a different wheat variety and claims that its bread now stays fresh for longer. Customers, it notes, are returning less bread as stale.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the bakery's claim?
options: A. The new flour costs slightly more than the flour it replaced.
B. The bakery reduced its prices at the same time as the change in flour.
C. Some customers say they prefer the taste of the new loaves.
D. The bakery's refund policy for stale bread was unchanged over the period.
E. The bakery sells more bread on weekdays than at weekends.
questions.explanation: The claim rests on returns as a proxy for staleness; an unchanged refund policy removes the obvious alternative explanation for fewer returns. C introduces a competing explanation, since cheaper bread may be eaten faster or returned less readily.

questions.prompt: In the Marnhill district, every household with a garden-waste subscription also has a recycling bin, and no household without a recycling bin composts at home. Most households that compost at home do not hold a garden-waste subscription.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: A. Most households in Marnhill have recycling bins.
B. Every household that composts at home has a recycling bin.
C. No household holds both a subscription and a compost heap.
D. Households with subscriptions produce less waste than those without.
E. Most households with recycling bins compost at home.
questions.explanation: From 'no household without a recycling bin composts' it follows that composting implies a recycling bin. A and E are unsupported claims about proportions of the whole district; C contradicts 'most', which permits some overlap; D introduces a quantity the statements never mention.

questions.prompt: A regional authority is deciding whether to fund a scheme collecting food waste separately from other household refuse, on the grounds that it will reduce the volume sent to landfill.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the scheme?
options: A. Whether residents of other regions support similar schemes
B. How many vehicles the authority currently owns
C. Whether the scheme would be popular with residents
D. What the scheme would be called in publicity material
E. Whether the collected food waste would be processed in a facility that itself sends residue to landfill in comparable volumes
questions.explanation: The stated objective is landfill volume; if processing merely relocates the material, the objective is not met. Popularity and branding bear on adoption, not on whether the goal is achieved.

questions.prompt: A survey of members at a chain of gyms found that members who attend early-morning sessions report higher job satisfaction than those who attend in the evening. The chain's marketing department concluded that exercising early in the day improves people's attitude to their work.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. relies on a survey with too few respondents to be meaningful
B. assumes that a difference between two self-selected groups was produced by the feature that distinguishes them
C. confuses job satisfaction with productivity
D. fails to define what counts as early morning
E. generalises from gym members to the population at large
questions.explanation: People choose their session time, and whatever leads someone to be free and willing at six in the morning — job autonomy, seniority, shift pattern — may be what raises satisfaction. E is a real limitation but the conclusion is about people who exercise, not the population.

questions.prompt: An online clothing retailer introduced a sizing tool that recommends a size from the customer's measurements. In the year after its introduction, the proportion of orders returned rose.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains this result?
options: A. The tool was used by fewer than half of customers.
B. Returns are processed by an external contractor.
C. The retailer's total sales fell slightly over the period.
D. The tool was introduced together with free returns, which drew a large number of new customers who habitually order two sizes and return one.
E. Competitors offer similar tools.
questions.explanation: It supplies a change in the customer mix that raises the return rate for reasons unrelated to sizing accuracy — the tool may work and the proportion still rise. A would explain a lack of improvement, not an increase.

questions.prompt: Firms that have adopted a four-day working week report output per employee equal to or greater than before the change. An analyst concludes that shortening the working week raises productivity.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the analyst's conclusion?
options: A. The firms that adopted the change were disproportionately those already running well enough to absorb the risk of trying it.
B. Employees at these firms report improved wellbeing.
C. Some firms extended daily hours slightly when they shortened the week.
D. Output was measured by the firms themselves.
E. A minority of firms returned to a five-day week.
questions.explanation: Selection: if the adopters were already high-performing, their output figures reflect the firms rather than the schedule. C and D weaken more mildly by muddying the measurement; B undermines the causal claim itself.

questions.prompt: Airline executives have argued that replacing an ageing fleet with new aircraft will reduce the airline's total fuel consumption, since the new aircraft burn less fuel per seat-kilometre.
questions.question: The argument assumes which of the following?
options: A. Fuel prices will not fall in the near future.
B. Passengers prefer to fly on newer aircraft.
C. The airline will not expand the number of seat-kilometres it flies enough to offset the per-unit saving.
D. The new aircraft will require less maintenance.
E. Other airlines will make similar replacements.
questions.explanation: A per-unit improvement reduces a total only if the number of units does not grow to compensate — the classic gap between efficiency and consumption. The other choices bear on cost or competition, not on the arithmetic of the total.

questions.prompt: Along a stretch of coast where sea otters have returned, kelp forests have expanded. Ecologists propose that otters cause the expansion by preying on sea urchins, which graze kelp.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologists' explanation?
options: A. Kelp grows more rapidly in cooler water.
B. Sea otters also eat crabs and molluscs.
C. Kelp forests support commercially valuable fish.
D. Otter populations remain below their historic levels.
E. Along comparable stretches of coast where otters remain absent, urchin numbers have risen and kelp has continued to decline.
questions.explanation: A parallel case in which the proposed cause is absent and the effect does not occur is the strongest available support short of experiment. B mildly weakens by diluting the mechanism; A offers a rival cause.

questions.prompt: Critics of a proposed reservoir argue that it should not be built because the valley it would flood contains rare plant communities. A supporter of the scheme replies that the critics own homes supplied by the existing reservoir network, and so are in no position to object.
questions.question: The supporter's reply is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: A. relies on evidence about plant communities that has not been verified
B. addresses the critics' circumstances rather than the substance of their argument
C. assumes that water demand will continue to grow
D. overlooks the cost of constructing the reservoir
E. treats a scientific question as though it were a political one
questions.explanation: Whether the critics benefit from existing reservoirs has no bearing on whether flooding this valley is justified — the reply attacks the arguer rather than the argument.

questions.passageText:
Managers are routinely advised to discontinue product lines that fail to cover their allocated costs, and the advice is often sound. Yet firms with sophisticated accounting frequently retain such lines deliberately, and the reasoning is not sentimental.

The first consideration is allocation itself. Overhead assigned to a line does not usually disappear when the line is dropped; it is redistributed across the remaining products, which then appear less profitable in turn. A sequence of individually defensible discontinuations can therefore leave a firm smaller and no more profitable, a pattern common enough in the management literature to have acquired a name.

The second consideration is demand interdependence. Where customers buy a bundle, the margin on any single item is a poor guide to its contribution. A supplier of industrial fasteners may lose money on unusual sizes and keep them because purchasing departments prefer a single source; a bookshop's loss-making reference section may draw the traffic on which the profitable sections depend.

The third is optionality. A line that is unprofitable at current volumes may be the firm's only presence in a market that could grow, and re-entry after exit is typically far more expensive than continued presence, because distribution relationships and regulatory approvals must be rebuilt.

None of this argues that unprofitable lines should be retained as a rule. It argues that the accounting figure is the beginning of the analysis rather than its conclusion, and that the relevant question is not whether a line covers its allocated costs but what would actually change if it were gone.
questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: A. argue that unprofitable product lines should generally be retained
B. describe how overhead is allocated in multi-product firms
C. compare the profitability of industrial suppliers and retailers
D. explain why the accounting profitability of a line may be a poor basis for discontinuing it
E. recommend a method for calculating the true cost of a product line
questions.explanation: The passage repeatedly qualifies its own case — it does not argue for retention as a rule, and explicitly says the accounting figure begins rather than ends the analysis. Choice A overstates; C and D describe details used as support.

questions.passageTitle: Residues and the Dating of Early Pottery
questions.passageText:
For most of the twentieth century, the earliest pottery was assumed to belong to settled farming communities, on the reasonable grounds that fragile, heavy vessels seemed ill-suited to mobile life. Two developments have unsettled that assumption.

The first is radiocarbon dating of sherds from sites in East Asia, which places some pottery well before the local adoption of agriculture — among hunting and fishing populations rather than farmers. The second, and more informative, is the chemical analysis of residues absorbed into the porous walls of the vessels themselves. Lipids trapped in the fabric can be extracted and their carbon isotopes measured, distinguishing marine from terrestrial sources and, in some cases, identifying the processing of aquatic foods.

The results have shifted the question from when pottery appeared to what it was for. Vessels from several early Japanese sites carry residues consistent with the intensive processing of fish, suggesting that the earliest ceramics were a technology for extracting oils and rendering foods storable, rather than a by-product of sedentary living.

Caution is warranted. Residue analysis samples what was cooked most often or most recently, not the full range of use, and vessels may be reused for purposes their makers did not intend. Absence of a lipid signal is weak evidence of absence, since preservation varies with soil chemistry. What the technique establishes securely is narrower than the headlines suggest: not that pottery was invented for fish, but that at particular sites it was used for them, early and repeatedly.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the assumption linking early pottery to farming was
options: A. reasonable given the evidence available but not supported by later findings
B. never seriously held by archaeologists
C. based on a misreading of radiocarbon dates
D. confirmed by residue analysis of East Asian sherds
E. derived from ethnographic study of mobile populations
questions.explanation: The passage calls the grounds reasonable, then describes two developments that unsettled the assumption. B captures both halves; the other choices contradict one or the other.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the inference that early Japanese vessels were used chiefly for processing fish?
options: A. Some of the sites analysed also contain fishing equipment
B. Radiocarbon dates from the sites are consistent with one another
C. Similar vessels from later periods carry the same residues
D. Lipids from aquatic foods survive in ceramic fabric far longer than lipids from plants or land animals
E. The vessels are thicker-walled than later cooking pots

questions.passageText:
The textbook prediction is straightforward: a wage floor above the market-clearing rate reduces employment. A substantial body of empirical work has failed to find that effect at the moderate increases actually legislated, and the resulting debate has been unusually productive.

One line of explanation invokes monopsony. Where employers face little competition for particular workers — because of geography, limited information, or the cost to workers of switching jobs — a firm sets wages below the value of the marginal worker's output and hires fewer workers than a competitive market would. In that setting a minimum wage can raise both pay and employment, up to a point, because it removes the firm's incentive to restrict hiring in order to hold wages down.

Critics respond that monopsony is invoked too freely, and that adjustment may occur along margins the studies do not measure: hours rather than headcount, scheduling flexibility, training, non-wage benefits, or slower future hiring rather than present dismissal. The disagreement is therefore less about whether firms respond than about where the response appears and how quickly.

What has emerged is a qualified consensus with a clear boundary condition. Moderate increases in low-wage labour markets have shown small employment effects; nothing in the evidence licenses extrapolation to floors far above prevailing local wages, and the studies that find little effect are studies of increases that were, by design, not extreme.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that under monopsony a minimum wage can raise employment because it
options: A. removes the firm's incentive to restrict hiring in order to hold wages down
B. increases consumer demand for the firm's products
C. compels firms to invest in training
D. reduces the cost to workers of switching jobs
E. eliminates competition among employers
questions.explanation: Stated directly. D describes a cause of monopsony, not the mechanism by which the floor operates; E reverses the situation being described.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the critics' position as presented in the passage?
options: A. Firms do not respond to wage floors at all
B. Monopsony has been disproved by recent studies
C. Adjustment may occur along margins the studies do not measure
D. Employment effects are large but temporary
E. Minimum wages should be set by local rather than national authorities
questions.explanation: The critics' claim is about where the response shows up — hours, scheduling, training, future hiring — not whether it occurs. A contradicts them; the passage says the dispute is less about whether firms respond.

questions.passageText:
Before the 1840s, clocks in British towns were set by local solar noon, so that Bristol ran some ten minutes behind London. The discrepancy was harmless while the fastest traffic moved at the speed of a horse. Railways ended that.

A timetable is a promise about simultaneity, and a network cannot make one across towns keeping different time. Railway companies therefore adopted London time on their own lines, printed it in their timetables, and in effect exported it along the track. Adoption by towns followed the railway rather than preceding it, and the sequence matters: standard time was not imposed by government and then used by industry, but adopted by industry and only later ratified in law, in Britain some four decades after the railways began the practice.

Resistance was neither trivial nor irrational. Local time was tied to the sun and to the authority of those who kept it, and its replacement transferred a small piece of civic autonomy to a private company. Some town clocks were fitted with two minute hands as a compromise, showing local and railway time together.

The episode is often cited as a case of technology dictating social arrangement. The more exact reading is that the technology made an existing inconsistency expensive. Local time had always been inconsistent; only when the cost of that inconsistency was borne by a coordinated network did anyone find it intolerable.
questions.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: A. the technical difficulties of building railway timetables
B. how and why standard time replaced local time, and how that case should be interpreted
C. the legal history of time regulation in Britain
D. public resistance to nineteenth-century technology
E. differences between solar time and mean time
questions.explanation: The passage narrates the change and then argues about its correct interpretation in the last paragraph. C and D are components of that account, not its subject.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the author's view of the claim that technology dictated the new arrangement?
options: A. It is imprecise: the technology made a long-standing inconsistency expensive rather than creating a new problem
B. It is correct, since the railways compelled towns to change
C. It is unfounded, since the change was legislated by government
D. It is unverifiable, since records of local timekeeping are incomplete
E. It is true of Britain but of no other country
questions.explanation: The passage offers the 'more exact reading' explicitly: inconsistency had always existed; the network made its cost intolerable.

Lipids trapped in the fabric can be extracted and their carbon isotopes measured, distinguishing marine from terrestrial sources and, in some cases, identifying the processing of aquatic foods.

The results have shifted the question from when pottery appeared to what it was for. Vessels from several early Japanese sites carry residues consistent with the intensive processing of fish, suggesting that the earliest ceramics were a technology for extracting oils and rendering foods storable, rather than a by-product of sedentary living.

Caution is warranted. Residue analysis samples what was cooked most often or most recently, not the full range of use, and vessels may be reused for purposes their makers did not intend. Absence of a lipid signal is weak evidence of absence, since preservation varies with soil chemistry. What the technique establishes securely is narrower than the headlines suggest: not that pottery was invented for fish, but that at particular sites it was used for them, early and repeatedly.

readingPassages.title: Monopsony and the Minimum Wage
readingPassages.text:
The textbook prediction is straightforward: a wage floor above the market-clearing rate reduces employment. A substantial body of empirical work has failed to find that effect at the moderate increases actually legislated, and the resulting debate has been unusually productive.

One line of explanation invokes monopsony. Where employers face little competition for particular workers — because of geography, limited information, or the cost to workers of switching jobs — a firm sets wages below the value of the marginal worker's output and hires fewer workers than a competitive market would. In that setting a minimum wage can raise both pay and employment, up to a point, because it removes the firm's incentive to restrict hiring in order to hold wages down.

Critics respond that monopsony is invoked too freely, and that adjustment may occur along margins the studies do not measure: hours rather than headcount, scheduling flexibility, training, non-wage benefits, or slower future hiring rather than present dismissal. The disagreement is therefore less about whether firms respond than about where the response appears and how quickly.

What has emerged is a qualified consensus with a clear boundary condition. Moderate increases in low-wage labour markets have shown small employment effects; nothing in the evidence licenses extrapolation to floors far above prevailing local wages, and the studies that find little effect are studies of increases that were, by design, not extreme.

readingPassages.title: The Standardisation of Time
readingPassages.text:
Before the 1840s, clocks in British towns were set by local solar noon, so that Bristol ran some ten minutes behind London. The discrepancy was harmless while the fastest traffic moved at the speed of a horse. Railways ended that.

A timetable is a promise about simultaneity, and a network cannot make one across towns keeping different time. Railway companies therefore adopted London time on their own lines, printed it in their timetables, and in effect exported it along the track. Adoption by towns followed the railway rather than preceding it, and the sequence matters: standard time was not imposed by government and then used by industry, but adopted by industry and only later ratified in law, in Britain some four decades after the railways began the practice.

Resistance was neither trivial nor irrational. Local time was tied to the sun and to the authority of those who kept it, and its replacement transferred a small piece of civic autonomy to a private company. Some town clocks were fitted with two minute hands as a compromise, showing local and railway time together.

The episode is often cited as a case of technology dictating social arrangement. The more exact reading is that the technology made an existing inconsistency expensive. Local time had always been inconsistent; only when the cost of that inconsistency was borne by a coordinated network did anyone find it intolerable.
